title: The widow's two mites (Mark 12:18–44)
hookLine: the great commandment, then a widow gives everything she has

lines: A WIDOW WITH TWO TINY COINS.
cards: The collection basket comes down the row at Mass. Some people drop in an envelope. Some tap their phone.
A kid puts in a quarter his mom handed him. Nobody's watching, or so you hope. Today, somebody is.
Jesus is still in the Temple, still being questioned. Then the questions stop, and he sits down across from the treasury, where people drop their offerings into the collection chests, and watches.
Rich people put in large amounts. Then a poor widow walks up with two tiny coins.

teach.h: THE SHEMA: LOVE WITH YOUR WHOLE HEART.
teach.b: First, the greatest commandment. A scribe asks which commandment is first of all. Jesus answers with the Shema, words Jews still pray today.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God." Love him with your whole heart, soul, mind and strength. And the second: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
The scribe agrees, and Jesus tells him: "Thou art not far from the kingdom of God." In Mark, a warm moment between Jesus and a scribe. Second, a warning.

teach.h: BEWARE THOSE WHO DEVOUR WIDOWS' HOUSES.
teach.b: Right after, Jesus warns about scribes who love long robes and the best seats, and who devour the houses of widows. Third, the widow. She drops in "two mites, which make a farthing."
Mites were lepta, tiny copper coins.
Jesus calls his disciples over: "this poor widow hath cast in more than all they who have cast into the treasury."
The rich gave from what they had left over.

teach.h: SHE OF HER WANT CAST IN ALL SHE HAD.
teach.b: She, out of her want, "cast in all she had, even her whole living." Fourth, two ways to hear it. The traditional reading hears praise: whole-heart love, the commandment lived out with two coins.
Some readers also hear a lament, since the story sits right after the warning about those who devour widows' houses: a system that takes a poor woman's last coins.
The two readings can stand together: the widow is honored, and those who would take from her are warned. Either way, Jesus measures her gift by what it cost her, not by the amount.

how: Catholics give at the offertory of the Mass and through almsgiving, one of the three traditional practices of Lent alongside prayer and fasting, and the Church teaches special care for widows and the poor.

games.q: you're sitting beside Jesus at the treasury. rich people drop in large sums. a poor widow drops in two tiny coins. who gave the most?
games.why: "this poor widow hath cast in more than all they who have cast into the treasury." she gave from her want: all she had.

practice: Ask yourself what a two-coin gift would be for you today: not a big donation, something small you'd actually feel, like your lunch hour for someone who needs to talk, the last of the good coffee, a few dollars you were saving, an apology that costs your pride.
Pick one, picture giving it, and notice the little pinch. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Mites. Two tiny copper coins, lepta in Greek, that a poor widow dropped into the treasury: more, Jesus said, than all the rich gave. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: two lepta, small copper coins. the old English is mites.

carryVoice: Your line: all she had. Two coins, and Jesus called it more than all the rest. Day two hundred twenty-three, done.
